title: Willow oval bread basket
subtitle: Basketry: an oval-base willow basket in brown willow, sized for a standard loaf
excerpt: An oval willow bread basket with a wrapped rand border, made from brown (boiled) buff willow. The oval base uses a slath construction; the sides are staked up and woven in four-rod wale, finished with a trac border. A working basket for daily kitchen use, sized to hold a standard tin loaf.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the oval slath construction; Twining, Basketwork for Beginners (1920) for the four-rod wale and trac border.

glossaryTerms.definition: The base framework of a willow basket, made by threading rods through a central bundle to form a cross or oval structure.
A weaving pattern using multiple rods that chase each other around the basket, creating a strong structural row.
A simple woven border where each stake is bent and threaded behind the neighbouring stakes to form a neat finished top edge.
Willow that has been boiled in water to fix a warm tan colour, then stripped of bark. The standard material for traditional English willow baskets.
A pointed metal tool for opening gaps in basketry weave to thread new rods.

content.text: A willow bread basket is a straight woven oval with a flat base, straight sides, and a trac border, the simplest complete willow basket form, and the right first project before tackling shaped baskets or handles. The key construction decisions are already made: the oval base determines the footprint, the waling gives the sides their structure, and the trac border is the fastest border that makes a solid top edge. This basket is sized to hold a standard 800g tin loaf.

in mixed lengths. You need: 6 base sticks (60 cm, thick end, 8, 10 mm diameter), 8 base sticks (45 cm, medium), about 20 weavers for the base (45, 60 cm), 20 side stakes (90 cm), and about 60 weavers for the sides (various lengths, 60, 90 cm). Pre-soak all the willow in water: buff willow needs soaking overnight (8, 12 hours) and then a 30-minute rest wrapped in cloth before working. Dry willow snaps; properly soaked willow bends without breaking.
Bodkin for opening gaps in the weave.
Secateurs for cutting rods to length.
Side cutters for trimming ends flush.
Basket weights (optional): heavy stones or purpose-made weights to keep the base flat during weaving.

Step 2: Tie in and weave the base

Use two thin weavers to tie in the slath: work them together around the central cross, pairing in and out around the sticks for the first four rounds to lock the cross, then separate and work independently for the remaining base rounds. Work outward in a pairing weave until the base is solid and all sticks are held firmly. The finished base should be flat, use the basket weights to hold it down if it tries to dome upward.

Trim the base weavers flush. Cut a point on the butt end of each 90 cm side stake and push it firmly into the base weave alongside each base stick, pointing down. Tie the stakes loosely at the top with string to keep them vertical during the upsett row, the first waling round that bends the stakes upright.

to lock the upsett. Then work the body of the basket in simple randing, single weavers worked under and over each stake, until the sides reach 14 cm height. Finish with two more rounds of four-rod wale to lock the top edge before the border.

is worked by bending each stake in turn down and in front of one stake to the right, then behind the next, then out to the front. Work all the way around, threading the final stakes through the gaps made by the first stakes. Trim all ends flush with side cutters once the border is complete.
Let the basket dry completely before use, at least 48 hours in a dry room. The willow shrinks slightly as it dries and all the joints tighten. No finish is needed for a bread basket.

attrs.symptom: The base domes upward during weaving
attrs.cause: Base sticks are under tension from the weave and springing upward
attrs.fix: Place a heavy flat weight on the base during weaving. Alternatively, turn the base upside down after the first four rounds and continue weaving from the reverse side, the tension reverses and the base flattens.

attrs.symptom: Weavers snap when bent around the stakes
attrs.cause: Willow under-soaked; dried out during working
attrs.fix: Re-soak any dry weavers for 15 minutes. Keep unused weavers wrapped in a damp cloth throughout the session. Buff willow is the most forgiving of the willow types for soaking, it tolerates slightly over-soaking without going mushy.
